I really hate the notion that an audio guide is a neutral thing. So often people just take them, they click on it, they walk through the museum, but they're completely distracted from the work. I've had great experiences with audio guides where it really opens up the painting, opens up the sculpture, tells you all the history, all the anecdotes, all the things that you'd never know otherwise. But at the same time, I've also been to museums where I'm just looking at the screen of the audio guide, or the little number on the wall, that's not really a neutral thing. So I think it's very valuable as a tool, but as long as it's optional, as long as it's very well-designed, and it's very selective. But the moment that it takes away from that very physical experience of looking at an artwork, thinking, feeling, it's kind of an issue.
The main advantage of audio guides is that it really brings people into these artworks. A lot of artworks are quite obscure, they don't tell you what they mean. So audio guides can really explain iconography, context, materiality, provenance, controversies, all of these things. And they can translate that very specialist vocabulary into very accessible language. So it's very valuable. Especially for blind or low-vision people. You can get audio description tours. So they can experience visual art too. It's also very valuable for people who speak a different language. And for kids, for casual visitors, it can really make it into a story. It can give it characters, conflicts, discoveries, all of these things. And then, you can go at your own pace. You can replay it, pause it, skip it. So it's very valuable and very democratizing. But at the same time, this voice that you're listening to, it becomes a very strong authority. It tells you what to look at, what to see, what to pay attention to. And it assigns a very specific meaning to a painting that maybe would've been very moving or puzzling on its own. So you just kind of go through the museum like checking boxes. You look at one artwork, you hear the number, then you move on. You are very isolated with your headphones. You don't talk to the person next to you. And you don't discover things together. And then, a lot of times, the audio guides are very long, very detailed. You really get cognitively overloaded. You're listening more than you're looking. And it can be very annoying, especially with a technical glitch, with a bad interface, or with people around you. And not every work needs an audio guide. I think there's a lot of value in silence and in ambiguity and in slow looking. But, yeah, I think that if it's done very well, if it's optional, if it's very concise, very selective, and it's layered, so you can get a very brief orientation that invites questions rather than answers. That's very valuable. And then it can also be very direct. Instead of saying, this painting is about despair or about war, it says, look at the brushwork on the left, look at this detail. And then, you can also have multiple voices. So it's not only the curator, but maybe the artist, maybe a community member, maybe a critic. And you can take it as a scaffold, and then you can just listen for five minutes, then take it out, look at the painting. And that's kind of ideal. But I wouldn't say that it's a bad thing, just that it can go very wrong. I think that audio guides really help and open doors and make things more accessible. But I just don't want it to become a corridor, something that takes you from A to B and very prescribed. And I think that the ideal is that there's a rhythm of listening and looking, guidance and freedom. And if it helps you see better, then it works. If it prevents you from seeing, just turn it off.
